Antibiotics should be used **selectively rather than routinely** in acute diverticulitis, reserved for patients who are systemically unwell or at high risk of complications [doc1].

**Indications for antibiotic use:**

Antibiotic therapy is appropriate for patients who are systemically unwell (fever, severe left lower quadrant pain, peritonitis on exam, elevated white blood cell count), immunosuppressed, or have significant comorbidity [doc1]. The rationale has shifted: acute diverticulitis is now considered an inflammatory process rather than primarily an infectious one, and major trials have shown no clear benefit of routine antibiotic use [doc1].

**Evidence supporting selective use:**

The AVOD trial (623 patients with CT-verified acute uncomplicated left-sided diverticulitis) found no significant differences between antibiotic and non-antibiotic management at 12 months in time to recovery, hospital stay, complications, or recurrences [doc1]. An 11-year follow-up showed the same—no difference in complications, recurrences, surgeries, or colorectal cancer rates [doc1]. The DIABOLO trial (528 patients) and subsequent 2019 meta-analyses reached identical conclusions [doc1]. A 2020 placebo-controlled trial in hospitalized patients also found no differences in length of stay, readmission, need for surgery, or pain [doc1].

Antibiotics must cover gram-negative rods and anaerobes, particularly *Escherichia coli* and *Bacteroides fragilis* [doc1]. Typical outpatient regimens include:

- Fluoroquinolone and metronidazole
- Sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim and metronidazole  
- Amoxicillin/clavulanate

Outpatient treatment duration is 7–10 days, with clinical reassessment at 2–3 days and weekly thereafter until symptom resolution [doc1].

**Hospitalization criteria:**

Acute uncomplicated diverticulitis with sepsis, microperforation, immunosuppression, high fever, significant leukocytosis, peritonitis, advanced age, significant comorbidities, or failed outpatient treatment requires inpatient admission. Acute complicated diverticulitis (perforation, abscess, obstruction, or fistulization) warrants inpatient treatment [doc1].

Diclectin (doxylamine/pyridoxine) has a controversial place in therapy for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy—it is the only Health Canada-approved medication for this indication, but recent evidence questions its clinical benefit over single-agent pyridoxine alone [doc1][doc2].

**Evidence and Status:**
Although Diclectin has been used in Canada for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy (NVP) since 1957, reanalysis of the original trial data found no clinically important benefit over placebo for those with mild-to-moderate symptoms [doc2]. A 2018 re-evaluation incorporating previously unpublished data concluded there is no benefit of the doxylamine-pyridoxine combination versus placebo [doc2]. Despite this, a Health Canada safety review concluded that no changes to the safety information were warranted and that benefits continue to outweigh risks [doc1].

**Clinical Recommendation:**
Canadian and American guidelines still recommend the pyridoxine/doxylamine combination as a first-line option [doc1]. However, given the lack of additional clinical efficacy of the combination, a trial of single-entity pyridoxine (25 mg Q8H PO) is now considered a reasonable evidence-based approach prior to considering Diclectin [doc2].

**If Diclectin Is Used:**
The standard dosing is 1 tablet in the morning and afternoon (to control daytime symptoms) and 2 tablets at bedtime (to control morning symptoms), used on a regular rather than PRN basis [doc1]. Up to 12 tablets/day can be used in some cases [doc1]. The product should be tapered on discontinuation [doc1]. Monitoring should include assessment for sedation and anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, constipation), with reassessment if nausea and vomiting are not improved after 3 days or adverse effects are intolerable [doc1].

**Safety:**
Over 33 million pregnant patients worldwide have taken this combination and it has not been found to increase the risk of major malformations [doc1]. Patients should be counselled that despite its safety, Diclectin may not be effective and that symptoms usually resolve on their own [doc1].

- Symptoms persist without improvement for **>10 days** after the start of URTI symptoms, OR
- Symptoms worsen within 10 days after an initial period of improvement ("double sickening") [doc1]

**Important:** No individual symptom reliably predicts bacterial involvement—fever occurs in viral infection, and nasal discharge colour reflects white blood cells rather than bacteria [doc1].

## When Antibiotics Should Be Considered

**Symptom management alone is the preferred initial strategy** for uncomplicated acute rhinosinusitis [doc1]. Even when bacterial involvement is suspected, antibiotics at diagnosis may not be necessary. Two antibiotic-sparing strategies are recommended:

1. **Intranasal corticosteroid (INCS) trial**: A 72-hour trial may avoid the need for antibiotics in mild-to-moderate cases; if no improvement after 72 hours, consider adding antibiotics [doc1]
2. **Watchful waiting**: Defer antibiotics for up to 7 days after diagnosis while providing symptom management; reassessment is mandatory if illness persists or worsens [doc1]

## When Antibiotics Are Indicated

Antimicrobial therapy should be offered to patients experiencing:
- **Significant symptom severity** affecting quality of life (interfering with activity or sleep) [doc1]
- **Red-flag symptoms** suggesting complicated disease (altered mental status, periorbital edema, visual changes, neck stiffness, severe headache, systemic illness) [doc1]
